title-group.article-title: Inpatient outcomes associated with acute kidney injury among adults hospitalized with colorectal cancer.

contrib-group.aff: Southern Clinical Oncology Center, Atlanta, GA
Pacific Precision Medicine Institute, San Francisco, CA
Great Lakes Cancer Consortium, Detroit, MI

permissions.copyright-statement: © 2026 by American Society of Clinical Oncology

abstract.p: Background: Patients hospitalized with colorectal cancer frequently have complex medical comorbidities, but the clinical impact of concurrent acute kidney injury is not well defined. We examined inpatient outcomes and resource utilization associated with this complication. Methods: We analyzed the National Inpatient Sample for 2016–2021. Adult hospitalizations with a diagnosis of colorectal cancer were identified using ICD-10-CM codes and stratified by the presence or absence of acute kidney injury. Weighted national estimates were generated. Multivariable logistic and linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, race, payer, hospital characteristics, metastatic disease, and comorbidity burden. Results: Among an estimated 142,608 hospitalizations for colorectal cancer, 21,570 included acute kidney injury. Patients with the complication had a median age of 66 years, and 49.3% were female. Mean length of stay was 8.4 versus 4.7 days, and mean hospital charges were $101,520 versus $61,180. After adjustment, acute kidney injury was associated with higher odds of need for mechanical ventilation (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 3.7), sepsis (aOR 2.9), and in-hospital mortality (aOR 3.2). Conclusions: Concurrent acute kidney injury identifies a clinically vulnerable subgroup of hospitalized patients with colorectal cancer and is associated with greater morbidity, mortality, and resource use. Early recognition and coordinated oncologic and medical management may improve inpatient care. Research Sponsor: None.
